approved: National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Worker Screening Database) Bill 2019

The majority voted against an amendment to the usual [second reading motion](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html), which is "*that the bill be read a second time*" - which is parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill. This means the amendment failed. It was introduced by Lalor MP [Joanne Ryan](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/lalor/joanne_ryan) (Labor). ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"the House:* > > *(1) notes that, while the National Worker Screening Database will be an important tool to prevent some abuse occurring in the future, it can never investigate the crimes of the past; and* > > *(2) welcomes the fact that there will finally be a Royal Commission into Violence and Abuse of People with Disability".*

The speaker supported the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Worker Screening Database) Bill 2019 but criticised the government for a $4.6 billion underspend in the NDIS and systemic failures, citing cases such as a boy in Queensland relying on a wheelbarrow for transport and a woman in Penrith needing a GoFundMe page for a car.

The speaker argued the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Worker Screening Database) Bill is essential to close state-based screening loopholes and create a national database, citing 1,459 serious incident reports (including 496 abuse allegations and 62 sexual misconduct allegations) in six months, with $22 billion flowing annually through the NDIS and 90,000 new jobs expected.

The NDIS Amendment (Worker Screening Database) Bill 2019 establishes a national database for NDIS worker screening checks, funded at $13.6 million over four years with states contributing $6.8 million. It aims to provide portable clearances and ongoing monitoring of criminal history to protect participants from harm.
